A p-value is one of the most used and most misunderstood numbers in data work. This article builds it from scratch, computes it three ways, and shows exactly what it does and does not tell you.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- The precise definition of a p-value
- How to compute one for a two-sample test
- How to avoid the most common misinterpretations
:::

## Intuition

Imagine you flip a coin 100 times and get 62 heads. Is the coin biased? A p-value answers a narrower question: **if the coin were fair, how surprising would a result at least this extreme be?**

## The definition

Given a null hypothesis $H_0$ and a test statistic $T$, the p-value for an observed value $t_{\text{obs}}$ is

$$
p = \Pr\big(\,|T| \ge |t_{\text{obs}}| \;\big|\; H_0 \,\big)
$$ {#eq-pvalue}

A small $p$ from @eq-pvalue means the data would be unusual *if* $H_0$ were true.

For a two-sample comparison of means, Welch's statistic is

$$
t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}
$$ {#eq-welch}

::: {#def-significance}
## Significance level
The threshold $\alpha$ (often $0.05$) chosen **before** looking at the data. We reject $H_0$ when $p < \alpha$.
:::

## Seeing it

```{python}
#| label: fig-null
#| fig-cap: "Under the null, the t statistic follows a t distribution. The shaded tails are the p-value."
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

t_obs, df = 2.1, 58
x = np.linspace(-4.5, 4.5, 600)
y = stats.t.pdf(x, df)
p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_obs), df)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.plot(x, y, color="#4F46E5", lw=2)
for side in (x >= t_obs, x <= -t_obs):
    ax.fill_between(x, y, where=side, color="#4F46E5", alpha=.22)
ax.axvline(t_obs, color="#4F46E5", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(t_obs + .15, .3, f"t = {t_obs}\np = {p:.3f}", color="#161B26", fontsize=10)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("t statistic under $H_0$")
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The shaded area in @fig-null is the probability of a result at least as extreme as ours, assuming no real difference.

## Computing it

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Python
```python
from scipy import stats

control   = [12.1, 11.8, 12.6, 13.0, 11.5, 12.2]
treatment = [13.4, 12.9, 13.8, 14.1, 12.7, 13.5]

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(treatment, control, equal_var=False)  # Welch
print(f"t = {t:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")
```
## R
```r
control   <- c(12.1, 11.8, 12.6, 13.0, 11.5, 12.2)
treatment <- c(13.4, 12.9, 13.8, 14.1, 12.7, 13.5)
t.test(treatment, control, var.equal = FALSE)
```
## SQL
```sql
-- Welch t statistic from summary stats (p-value then from a t table or Python)
SELECT
  (AVG(CASE WHEN grp = 'treatment' THEN value END) -
   AVG(CASE WHEN grp = 'control'   THEN value END)) /
  SQRT(VAR_SAMP(CASE WHEN grp = 'treatment' THEN value END) / COUNT(CASE WHEN grp = 'treatment' THEN 1 END) +
       VAR_SAMP(CASE WHEN grp = 'control'   THEN value END) / COUNT(CASE WHEN grp = 'control'   THEN 1 END)) AS t_stat
FROM experiment;
```
:::

## Four common mistakes

| Mistake | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| "p is the probability $H_0$ is true" | p assumes $H_0$ is true; it cannot also measure it |
| "p > 0.05 proves no effect" | Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence |
| "Smaller p means a bigger effect" | p mixes effect size and sample size |
| Testing many metrics, reporting the best | Inflates false positives; correct for multiple tests |

: Misreadings to avoid {#tbl-mistakes}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Always report the effect size
Pair every p-value with an estimate and a confidence interval. A tiny, useless difference can be "significant" with enough data.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: p-values are uniform under the null
If $H_0$ is true and the test is exact, $p \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$. That is why $\Pr(p < 0.05 \mid H_0) = 0.05$ is exactly the false-positive rate.
:::

## The workflow

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  A[Choose H0 and alpha] --> B[Collect data] --> C[Compute statistic] --> D[p-value] --> E[Decide and report effect size]
```

## Summary

- A p-value is $\Pr(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, nothing more.
- Choose $\alpha$ before you look, and always report the effect size.
- Next: read about confidence intervals in *Statistical Inference*.

For a rigorous treatment, see @casella2002.[^1]

[^1]: Chapter 8 covers hypothesis testing in depth.
